title: How to measure what a price increase or policy change did to customer sentiment
summary: Go beyond the complaint spike: compare themes and sentiment before and after a price or policy change, by segment, and check if the theme mix shifted.
body_markdown:
You raised prices, changed a plan, or tightened a policy. The complaints arrived on schedule. Now someone in the leadership meeting asks the real question: did this change how customers feel about us, or was it a loud week? The complaint count can't answer that. It tells you how many people noticed the change. It doesn't tell you how many people now see you differently.


Measure it with a before-and-after comparison of feedback, split by segment. Compare the themes and sentiment from a stable period before the change with a period after the first reaction has settled. Separate the one-off complaint spike from lasting movement. Then check whether the mix of themes has shifted. A change in what customers talk about often matters more than a change in how loudly they talk. Thematic does this with its Score Change waterfall. It shows how much each theme and each segment contributed to a change in[net promoter score (NPS)](https://getthematic.com/insights/ultimate-guide-to-net-promoter-score) or[customer satisfaction (CSAT)](https://getthematic.com/insights/link-feedback-themes-nps-csat-drivers) between two periods.


Below is the five-step process, what each step looks like in practice, and the mistakes that most often lead teams to the wrong conclusion.


## The five-step process


1. **Fix your comparison windows.** Pick a clean "before" period and an "after" period that starts once the announcement wave has passed.
2. **Isolate the change themes.** Tag the feedback that is about the change itself, so you can measure it separately from everything else.
3. **Separate the spike from the shift.** Check whether the change themes and the overall score stay elevated or fall back toward baseline.
4. **Compare the theme mix, not just the volume.** Look for themes that grew or shrank in share, especially value, trust and fairness themes.
5. **Break it down by segment.** Find out which customers moved, and whether the overall score hides a group that moved a lot.


## Step 1: Fix your comparison windows


A before-and-after comparison is only as good as its two windows. The "before" window should be a normal stretch of feedback with no other major change in it. The "after" window should start once the first wave of reaction to the announcement has passed, so you are measuring the new normal rather than the news.


Set both windows before you look at the data. Choose them after you see the chart, and you'll end up proving whatever you already believed.


Check the calendar too. If your "after" window lands in a busier or quieter season than your "before" window, some of the movement will be seasonal. The guide on[telling a real trend from a seasonal one](https://getthematic.com/insights/real-trend-or-seasonal-customer-feedback) covers how to compare against the same period last year.


**Common mistake:** comparing the week after the announcement with the month before it. The windows are different lengths, and the week after captures reaction to the news, not the lasting effect of the change.


## Step 2: Isolate the change themes


Not every comment after a price change is about the price change. Separate the feedback that mentions the change directly (price, plan, fee, policy, notice) from the feedback that doesn't.


This gives you two questions instead of one. First, how do customers feel about the change itself? Second, has sentiment on everything else moved? The second question is the one that tells you whether the relationship changed. A customer who complains about the new fee but still praises your support is in a different place from a customer whose comments about support have turned negative too.


Thematic tags each part of a comment with its own themes and[sentiment score](https://getthematic.com/insights/sentiment-analysis-customer-experience) , so a single comment can carry a negative view of the price and a positive view of the product. That matters here, because price feedback is rarely all one thing.


**Common mistake:** treating every negative comment after the change as caused by the change. Some of it was there before.


## Step 3: Separate the spike from the shift


A complaint spike is normal. What matters is what happens after it.


Track the change themes and the overall score across several periods after the change. You are looking for one of three patterns:


- **Spike and recover.** Complaints rise, then fall back toward baseline, and the overall score returns to where it was. Customers noticed and moved on.
- **Spike and settle higher.** Complaints fall from their peak but stay above baseline. The change became a lasting source of friction.
- **Quiet slide.** Complaint volume is modest, but the score drifts down over several periods. This is the pattern teams miss most, because nothing looks like an emergency.


Thematic's Significant Changes view flags themes whose volume or score has moved more than two standard deviations from their recent average, filtered for statistical significance. That helps you tell a lasting shift from normal variation once a few periods of post-change data exist.


**Common mistake:** declaring victory when complaint volume drops. Volume can fall while sentiment stays lower than it was.


## Step 4: Compare the theme mix, not just the volume


The most useful signal after a pricing or policy change is often a change in *what* customers talk about, not how much they complain.


Compare the share of feedback each theme takes up in the before and after windows. Pay particular attention to:


- **Value themes.** Comments about whether the product is worth it. A rise here means customers are re-evaluating the trade, not only reacting to the number.
- **Fairness and trust themes.** Comments about how the change was made, explained or timed.
- **Themes the change exposed.** Existing problems customers now mention more because they are paying more or getting less flexibility.


Academic research on price increases supports this focus.[Homburg, Hoyer and Koschate (2005)](https://madoc.bib.uni-mannheim.de/22603/) found that customers' reactions depend on the perceived fairness of the motive behind an increase, not only its size, and that satisfaction before the change shapes both effects.


Thematic's Score Change waterfall shows this directly. It breaks the change in NPS or CSAT between two periods into the[contribution of each theme](https://getthematic.com/insights/nps-root-cause-analysis) . Themes that pushed the score up show in green. Themes that pulled it down show in red. The contributions add up to the total change in score.


**Common mistake:** reporting only the change theme. If "value for money" is now dragging the score, the change may have been absorbed on price but not on value.


## Step 5: Break it down by segment


A change imposed on every customer rarely lands the same way for every customer. A flat overall score can hide one segment that moved sharply and another that didn't move at all.


Split the before-and-after comparison by the segments the change affected differently: plan or tier, tenure, region, contract type, or customers on grandfathered terms. Then ask which segment accounts for most of the movement.


Thematic's Score Change tool can show this by segment. Pick a filter, and each bar shows how much that segment contributed to the change in score. Each bar includes both the change in that segment's score and the change in its share of responses. With the Compare with filter, you can set two segments side by side and compare their themes.


**Common mistake:** reading a stable overall score as "no impact". Check whether a high-value segment moved while a larger, less affected segment held the average up.


## How this differs from a product launch review


A[post-launch analysis](https://getthematic.com/insights/post-launch-analysis) looks at something customers chose to try. A price increase or policy change is imposed on customers whether they want it or not. That changes what you measure. After a launch, you mostly ask whether the new thing works. After an imposed change, you ask whether customers' view of the whole relationship moved. That's why Steps 2 and 4 look past the change itself to everything else customers say.


## Common mistakes to avoid


- **Measuring the spike and stopping.** The spike measures awareness. Measure the periods after it.
- **Using complaint count as the only metric.** Track score and theme mix as well.
- **Choosing windows after seeing the data.** Fix them in advance.
- **Ignoring seasonality.** Compare with the same period last year where you can.
- **Averaging across segments.** Break the result down by the groups the change affected differently.
- **Looking only at the change theme.** Check whether sentiment on unrelated themes moved too.


## In short: how to measure a price or policy change beyond the complaint spike


To measure what a price increase or policy change did to customer sentiment, compare feedback themes and sentiment before and after the change, by segment. Wait out the announcement spike. Then check whether the score recovered, whether value, fairness and trust themes grew, and which segments drove the change. Thematic's Score Change waterfall breaks that movement down by theme and by segment, so the answer to "what did the change do?" is a chart, not a guess.
